claim: Paclitaxel (Taxol) is a taxane and a chemotherapeutic drug that stabilizes microtubules.
source: Paclitaxel (Taxol) is a taxane and a chemotherapeutic drug that stabilizes microtubules.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by extensive literature and clinical use.

claim: The lack of high-resolution structural information on a tubulin-taxane complex precludes a comprehensive description of the binding determinants that affect its mechanism of action.
source: While the interaction of paclitaxel with microtubules is well described, the lack of high-resolution structural information on a tubulin-taxane complex precludes a comprehensive description of the binding determinants that affect its mechanism of action.
evidence: The authors state this as a gap in knowledge that motivates their study.

claim: The crystal structure of baccatin III-tubulin complex was solved at 1.9 Å resolution.
source: Here, we solved the crystal structure of baccatin III the core moiety of paclitaxel-tubulin complex at 1.9 Å resolution.
evidence: This is a direct experimental result reported in the manuscript, with crystallographic data provided in Table 1.

claim: Taxanes bind better to microtubules than to tubulin because tubulin assembly is linked to a βM-loop conformational reorganization that otherwise occludes the access to the taxane site.
source: The results sheds light on three main mechanistic questions: (1) taxanes bind better to microtubules than to tubulin because tubulin assembly is linked to a βM-loopconformational reorganization (otherwise occludes the access to the taxane site) and, bulky C13 side chains preferentially recognize the assembled conformational state
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from combined structural and computational analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Bulky C13 side chains preferentially recognize the assembled conformational state of tubulin.
source: The results sheds light on three main mechanistic questions: (1) taxanes bind better to microtubules than to tubulin because tubulin assembly is linked to a βM-loopconformational reorganization (otherwise occludes the access to the taxane site) and, bulky C13 side chains preferentially recognize the assembled conformational state
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons and binding studies with modified taxanes.

claim: The occupancy of the taxane site has no influence on the straightness of tubulin protofilaments.
source: (2) the occupancy of the taxane site has no influence on the straightness of tubulin protofilaments and
evidence: This conclusion is based on MD simulations showing curved protofilaments in both presence and absence of taxanes.

claim: Longitudinal expansion of the microtubule lattices arises from the accommodation of the taxane core within the site.
source: (3) longitudinal expansion of the microtubule lattices arises from the accommodation of the taxane core within the site, a process that is no related to the microtubule stabilization (baccatin III is biochemically inactive).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray fiber diffraction data and MD simulations showing displacement of the βS9-βS10 loop.

claim: Baccatin III is biochemically inactive.
source: (3) longitudinal expansion of the microtubule lattices arises from the accommodation of the taxane core within the site, a process that is no related to the microtubule stabilization (baccatin III is biochemically inactive).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations and binding studies showing lack of microtubule stabilization activity.

claim: Paclitaxel is included in the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines.
source: The taxane paclitaxel is a drug included in the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines (World Health Organization, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the WHO document.

claim: Taxanes are used for the treatment of several solid tumors, such as ovarian, lung, and breast cancer, as well as advanced Kaposi's sarcoma.
source: Taxanes, either alone or in combination with other chemotherapeutic agents, are important drugs for the treatment of several solid tumors, such as ovarian, lung, and breast cancer, as well as advanced Kaposi's sarcoma (Ettinger, 1993; Arbuck et al., 1994; Saville et al., 1995; Lindemann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Three taxanes in clinical use are paclitaxel (Taxol), docetaxel (Taxotere), and cabazitaxel (Jevtana).
source: The three taxanes in clinical use, paclitaxel (Taxol), docetaxel (Taxotere), and cabazitaxel (Jevtana), are part of a large family of chemically diverse compounds that bind to the so-called 'taxane site' of the αβ-tubulin heterodimer (Field et al., 2013; Steinmetz and Prota, 2018; Figure 1A and B), the building block of microtubules.
evidence: This is supported by literature citations and is established clinical knowledge.

claim: Taxanes bind to the 'taxane site' of the αβ-tubulin heterodimer.
source: The three taxanes in clinical use, paclitaxel (Taxol), docetaxel (Taxotere), and cabazitaxel (Jevtana), are part of a large family of chemically diverse compounds that bind to the so-called 'taxane site' of the αβ-tubulin heterodimer (Field et al., 2013; Steinmetz and Prota, 2018; Figure 1A and B), the building block of microtubules.
evidence: This is supported by literature citations and structural data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The appearance of peripheral sensory neuropathy and other side effects caused by taxanes compromises treatment efficacy in the long term.
source: However, the appearance of peripheral sensory neuropathy and other side effects caused by taxanes compromises treatment efficacy in the long term (Gornstein and Schwarz, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Taxane-site ligands stabilize microtubules and suppress their dynamics.
source: Because taxane-site ligands stabilize microtubules and suppress their dynamics, they are collectively called microtubule-stabilizing agents.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Several structures of microtubules in complex with taxane-site agents have been analyzed and solved by cryo-electron microscopy to resolutions ranging between ~3 and ~10 Å.
source: Several structures of microtubules in complex with taxane-site agents have been recently analyzed and solved by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to resolutions ranging between ~3 and ~10 Å.
evidence: This is a summary of recent structural studies in the field.

claim: Paclitaxel acts on longitudinal tubulin contacts along protofilaments in microtubules by allosterically expanding the microtubule lattice in the direction of its long filament axis.
source: For paclitaxel, it was initially suggested that the drug acts on longitudinal tubulin contacts along protofilaments in microtubules by allosterically expanding the microtubule lattice in the direction of its long filament axis (Vale et al., 1994; Arnal and Wade, 1995; Alushin et al., 2014), a notion that is also consistent with X-ray fiber diffraction data (Estévez-Gallego et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Paclitaxel enhances lattice flexibility and acts on lateral tubulin contacts between protofilaments in microtubules through interactions with the M-loop of the β-tubulin subunit.
source: However, more recent studies suggest that paclitaxel enhances lattice flexibility and acts on lateral tubulin contacts between protofilaments in microtubules through interactions with the M-loop of the β-tubulin subunit (βM loop) (Kellogg et al., 2017; Debs et al., 2020; Manka and Moores, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by recent literature citations.

claim: Taxane-site ligands have the capacity to bind to unassembled tubulin dimers and promote their assembly into microtubules.
source: Besides directly acting on microtubules, taxane-site ligands also have the capacity to bind to unassembled tubulin dimers and promote their assembly into microtubules (Schiff and Horwitz, 1981; Carlier and Pantaloni, 1983; Howard and Timasheff, 1988; Díaz et al., 1993; Buey et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Several structures of non-taxane agents bound to the taxane site of tubulin have been solved to resolutions ranging from 2.4 to 1.8Å by X-ray crystallography.
source: Several structures of non-taxane agents bound to the taxane site of tubulin have been solved to resolutions ranging from 2.4 to 1.8Å by X-ray crystallography (Prota et al., 2013a; Trigili et al., 2016; Prota et al., 2017; Balaguer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple literature citations to crystallographic studies.

claim: Zampanolide and epothilone A stabilize lateral tubulin contacts between protofilaments within microtubules by structuring and stabilizing the βM loop into a short α-helix.
source: These data suggested that one mode of action of some taxane-site ligands such as zampanolide (PDB ID 4I4T) or epothilone A (PDB ID 4I5O) on unassembled tubulin is to stabilize lateral tubulin contacts between protofilaments within microtubules by structuring and stabilizing the βM loop into a short α-helix (Prota et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation to structural studies.

claim: The absence of a helical structure for the βM loop segment in the presence of dictyostatin and discodermolide suggests a different mechanism of microtubule stabilization for these two classes of non-taxane agents.
source: In contrast, the absence of a helical structure for this segment in the presence of the taxane-site ligands dictyostatin (PDB ID 4MF4) and discodermolide (PDB ID 5LXT) (Trigili et al., 2016; Prota et al., 2017) suggests a different, still poorly understood mechanism of microtubule stabilization for these two classes of non-taxane agents.
evidence: This is supported by literature citations to structural studies.

claim: Tubulin displays two prominent conformations that are related to its assembly state: a 'straight' conformation present in assembled microtubules and a 'curved' conformation observed in unassembled tubulin.
source: It is well established that tubulin displays two prominent conformations that are related to its assembly state (reviewed in Knossow et al., 2020): a 'straight' conformation present in assembled microtubules (denoted 'straight tubulin' hereafter) and a 'curved' conformation observed in unassembled tubulin (denoted 'curved tubulin' hereafter).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a review citation.

claim: The 'curved-to-straight' conformational transition is required for the formation of lateral tubulin contacts between protofilaments in the main shaft of microtubules.
source: The 'curved-to-straight' conformational transition is required for the formation of lateral tubulin contacts between protofilaments in the main shaft of microtubules.
evidence: This is established knowledge about microtubule assembly.

claim: The activation mechanism of taxanes facilitates the curved-to-straight conformational transition by preferentially binding to the straight conformation of tubulin.
source: Some data suggest that the activation mechanism of taxanes facilitates the curved-to-straight conformational transition by preferentially binding to the straight conformation of tubulin (Nogales et al., 1998; Elie-Caille et al., 2007; Benoit et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Structural information of a taxane in complex with unassembled tubulin is currently unavailable.
source: Structural information of a taxane in complex with unassembled tubulin is currently unavailable.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The main reason for the differential affinity of taxane-site ligands for assembled tubulin and unassembled tubulin arises from the stabilization of the βM loop in an 'out' conformation compatible with the formation of specific lateral contacts in microtubules and the selectivity of the bulky C13 side chain for the assembled, straight conformational state of tubulin.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that the main reason for the differential affinity of taxane-site ligands for assembled tubulin and unassembled tubulin arises from two terms. First, the stabilization of the βM loop in an 'out' conformation compatible with the formation of specific lateral contacts in microtubules and second, the selectivity of the bulky C13 side chain for the assembled, straight conformational state of tubulin.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined experimental and computational results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The occupancy of the taxane site results in a displacement of the S9-S10 loop of β-tubulin that accounts for the observed microtubule expansion with no influence on the straightness of tubulin protofilaments.
source: Finally, we found that the occupancy of the taxane site results in a displacement of the S9-S10 loop of β-tubulin that accounts for the observed microtubule expansion with no influence, however, on the straightness of tubulin protofilaments.
evidence: This conclusion is based on MD simulations and structural analyses.

claim: Baccatin III shows detectable affinity (Kb 25°C 3.0±0.5 × 10³ M⁻¹) to unassembled tubulin.
source: We found that baccatin III shows detectable affinity (Kb 25°C 3.0±0.5 × 103 M–1) to unassembled tubulin, which is in the same range as for other compounds that have been co-crystallized with tubulin, such as epothilone A 8±3 × 103 M–1 (Canales et al., 2014) and discodermolide 2.0±0.7 × 104 M–1 (Canales et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a direct experimental measurement reported in the manuscript.

claim: The T2R-TTL-baccatin III complex structure was solved at 1.9 Å resolution (PDB ID 8BDE).
source: Subsequently, we succeeded in obtaining a T2R-TTL-baccatin III complex structure that was solved at 1.9 Å resolution (PDB ID 8BDE) (Figure 2A and D; Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with crystallographic data provided in Table 1 and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Baccatin III binds to the taxane site of curved tubulin with its C2-benzoyloxy ring C stacked between the side chains of βH229 and βL275 in the leucine-rich β-tubulin pocket.
source: We found that the ligand binds to the taxane site of curved tubulin with its C2-benzoyloxy ring C stacked between the side chains of βH229 and βL275 in the leucine-rich β-tubulin pocket lined by the side chains of βC213, βL217, βL219, βD226, βH229, βL230, and βL275 (Figures 3A and 4A).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure analysis shown in Figures 3A and 4A.

claim: The carbonyl oxygen of baccatin III forms a weak hydrogen bond to the main chain amide of βR278.
source: Its carbonyl oxygen forms a weak hydrogen bond to the main chain amide of βR278.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The C10 acetate of baccatin III is exposed to the solvent and, together with the C12 methyl, is within van der Waals distance to βG370 of the βS9-βS10 loop.
source: The C10 acetate is exposed to the solvent and, together with the C12 methyl, is within van der Waals distance to βG370 of the βS9-βS10 loop.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The oxetane oxygen and the C13 hydroxyl of baccatin III accept hydrogen bonds from the main chain amide nitrogen of βT276 and the βH229 imidazole NE2, respectively.
source: Furthermore, the oxetane oxygen and the C13 hydroxyl accept hydrogen bonds from the main chain amide nitrogen of βT276 and the βH229 imidazole NE2, respectively.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The C4 acetate of baccatin III is buried in the hydrophobic pocket made up by βL230, βA233, βF272, βP274, βL275, βM302, βL371, and the aliphatic portion of the βR369 side chain.
source: The C4 acetate is buried in the hydrophobic pocket made up by βL230, βA233, βF272, βP274, βL275, βM302, βL371, and the aliphatic portion of the βR369 side chain.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Compound 2a binds to unassembled tubulin dimers with Kb25°C 0.8±0.3 × 10³ M⁻¹.
source: We could measure binding of 2a to unassembled tubulin dimers (Kb25°C 0.8±0.3 × 103 M–1), but not of N-AB-PT (Li et al., 2000), Chitax 40 (Matesanz et al., 2008), or Chitax 68 (Ma et al., 2018), thus indicating that the modification of the paclitaxel structure increased the binding affinity for unassembled tubulin.
evidence: This is a direct experimental measurement reported in the manuscript.

claim: The modification of the paclitaxel structure in compound 2a increased the binding affinity for unassembled tubulin.
source: We could measure binding of 2a to unassembled tubulin dimers (Kb25°C 0.8±0.3 × 103 M–1), but not of N-AB-PT (Li et al., 2000), Chitax 40 (Matesanz et al., 2008), or Chitax 68 (Ma et al., 2018), thus indicating that the modification of the paclitaxel structure increased the binding affinity for unassembled tubulin.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of binding measurements.

claim: The T2R-TTL-2a complex structure was refined to 1.95 Å resolution (PDB ID 8BDF).
source: In fact (Figure 2B, C, E and F), we found unequivocal difference electron densities at the taxane site of β-tubulin in T2R-TTL crystals soaked with 2a (PDB ID 8BDF) and 2b (PDB ID 8BDG) and refined the corresponding structures to 1.95 and 2.35 Å resolution, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with crystallographic data provided in Table 1.

claim: The T2R-TTL-2b complex structure was refined to 2.35 Å resolution (PDB ID 8BDG).
source: In fact (Figure 2B, C, E and F), we found unequivocal difference electron densities at the taxane site of β-tubulin in T2R-TTL crystals soaked with 2a (PDB ID 8BDF) and 2b (PDB ID 8BDG) and refined the corresponding structures to 1.95 and 2.35 Å resolution, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with crystallographic data provided in Table 1.

claim: Compounds 2a and 2b do not form covalent adducts with β-tubulin.
source: For further validation, we collected additional X-ray diffraction data on T2R-TTL crystals soaked with the haloacetamide derivative 2b at the bromine peak wavelength of 0.91501 Å. After rigid body and restrained refinement, we detected two clear anomalous difference peaks in electron densities at the taxane sites of the two tubulin dimers in the T2R-TTL crystals soaked with 2b (Figure 2G), which did not support covalent bond formation.
evidence: This is based on anomalous diffraction data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The continuous electron density observed in the T2R-TTL-2a structure represents a strong hydrogen bond between the βH229 NE2 and the C39 carbonyl of the ligand side chain rather than a covalent bond.
source: Accordingly, we interpreted the continuous electron density observed in the T2R-TTL-2a structure as a strong hydrogen bond between the βH229 NE2 and the C39 carbonyl of the ligand side chain rather than a covalent bond (Figure 3B).
evidence: This interpretation is based on refinement results and electron density analysis.

claim: Compound 2a engages in comparable interactions to curved tubulin by means of both its C2-benzoyloxy ring C and its oxetane moieties, as found for baccatin III.
source: The T2R-TTL-2a complex structure revealed that 2a engages in comparable interactions to curved tubulin by means of both its C2-benzoyloxy ring C and its oxetane moieties, as found for baccatin III (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 3.

claim: The core ring system of 2a is tilted toward helix βH6 and strand βS7 by ~20° compared to baccatin III.
source: However, the core ring system of 2a is tilted toward helix βH6 and strand βS7 by ~20° (angle between the two C1-C9 axes; rmsdbacIII-2a of 0.794 Å for 39 core atoms), thereby adopting a pose that is closer to that observed for paclitaxel bound to straight tubulin in microtubules (PDB ID 6WVR; rmsd2a-paclitaxel of 0.845 Å for 56 core atoms; rmsdbacIII-paclitaxel of 1.048 Å for 42 core atoms; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and RMSD calculations.

claim: The C39 carbonyl of the C13-3'-N-acrylamide moiety of 2a forms a hydrogen bond to the βH229 NE2 in curved tubulin, similar to paclitaxel bound to straight tubulin.
source: Similar to paclitaxel bound to straight tubulin, the C39 carbonyl of the C13-3'-N-acrylamide moiety of 2a forms a hydrogen bond to the βH229 NE2 in curved tubulin (Figures 3B and 4B).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figures 3B and 4B.

claim: The terminal ester moiety of 2a is exposed to the solvent and forms water-mediated hydrogen bonds to the side chains of βE22 and βR369 of β-tubulin.
source: The terminal ester moiety of 2a is exposed to the solvent and it forms water-mediated hydrogen bonds to the side chains of βE22 and βR369 of β-tubulin; it lodges within a space that is otherwise occupied by crystallographic water molecules in the curved tubulin-baccatin III structure.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The favorable hydrogen bond network established by 2a cannot be established by the 3'-N-benzamido phenyl ring A of paclitaxel in the curved tubulin conformation.
source: This favorable hydrogen bond network cannot be established by the 3'-N-benzamido phenyl ring A of paclitaxel in the curved tubulin conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison.

claim: In the context of paclitaxel-bound microtubules, helix H1 moves closer toward helix H7, allowing side chains of Lys19, Glu22, and Val23 to form a hydrophobic cavity that stabilizes the A ring.
source: In the context of paclitaxel-bound microtubules (straight tubulin), the helix H1 moves closer toward helix H7, thereby allowing these three side chains to form a hydrophobic cavity that stabilizes the A ring, which suggest a structural mechanism for the higher affinity of paclitaxel observed for the straight tubulin conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison between curved and straight tubulin conformations.

claim: The helix H1 movement causes the side chain of βD26 to occupy the space of the βR369 side chain, which adopts a flipped-out conformation, providing additional stabilization through a polar interaction to the 3' amide nitrogen of paclitaxel.
source: Moreover, the helix H1 movement causes the side chain of βD26 to occupy the space of the βR369 side chain, which adopts a flipped-out conformation. This arrangement provides additional stabilization through a polar interaction to the 3' amide nitrogen of paclitaxel and supports a more favorable binding of paclitaxel to microtubules (Figures 3B and 4B).
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison shown in Figures 3B and 4B.

claim: The absence of the C10 acetate in 2a relative to baccatin III has little impact on the conformation of the secondary structural elements that shape the taxane site.
source: The absence of the C10 acetate in 2a relative to baccatin III has little impact on the conformation of the secondary structural elements that shape the taxane site (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The main interaction energy of taxanes is mediated by their common baccatin III core moieties.
source: Together, these structural data provide – for the first time – a high-resolution structural description of the interaction of taxanes harboring a C13 side chain with unassembled, curved tubulin. They indicate that the main interaction energy of this class of antitubulin agents is mediated by their common baccatin III core moieties.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data presented.

claim: The taxane pose in both curved and straight tubulin is very similar.
source: They further reveal that the taxane pose in both curved and straight tubulin is very similar; however, subtle structural details reveal why paclitaxel binds more favorably to straight tubulin.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Significant conformational changes were observed for backbone atoms of the βT5 loop and the N-terminal segment of the βM loop in both the tubulin-baccatin III and tubulin-2a complex structures.
source: As shown in Figure 5, significant and comparable conformational changes were observed for backbone atoms of the βT5 loop and the N-terminal segment of the βM loop in both the tubulin-baccatin III and tubulin-2a complex structures.
evidence: This is based on RMSD analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The βT5 loop is oriented in the active 'out' conformation in both tubulin-baccatin III and tubulin-2a structures.
source: Interestingly, the βT5 loop that is prominently involved in establishing longitudinal tubulin contacts along protofilaments is oriented in the active 'out' conformation in both structures (Nawrotek et al., 2011).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures and supported by a literature citation.

claim: There is an allosteric crosstalk between the taxane site and the βT5 loop possibly via the central helix βH7 and the guanosine nucleotide bound to β-tubulin.
source: This observation indicates an allosteric crosstalk between the taxane site and the βT5 loop possibly via the central helix βH7 and the guanosine nucleotide bound to β-tubulin.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: Well-defined electron densities for the βM loop were found only for its N-terminal section up to residue βR278, while the remaining portion of the loop appeared disordered in both baccatin III and 2a complex structures.
source: In the case of the βM loop, we only found well-defined electron densities for its N-terminal section up to residue βR278, while the remaining portion of the loop appeared disordered in both complex structures.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures.

claim: Partial βM loop structuring has been observed previously in tubulin complexes with the taxane-site ligands dictyostatin and discodermolide.
source: This partial βM loop structuring has been observed previously in tubulin complexes with the taxane-site ligands dictyostatin and discodermolide (Trigili et al., 2016; Prota et al., 2017; note that the taxane-site ligands zampanolide and epothilone A promote the structuring of the βM loop into a helical conformation Prota et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: A direct effect of taxanes on the βM loop is consistent with the notion that paclitaxel stabilizes this secondary structural element in two discrete conformations giving rise to heterogeneous lateral microtubule-lattice contacts.
source: A direct effect of taxanes on the βM loop is consistent with the notion that paclitaxel stabilizes this secondary structural element in two discrete conformations giving rise to heterogeneous lateral microtubule-lattice contacts (Debs et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Significant conformational changes were found in the βS9-βS10 loop, which were more prominent in tubulin-2a than in tubulin-baccatin III.
source: We also found significant conformational changes in the βS9-βS10 loop, which were more prominent in tubulin-2a than in tubulin-baccatin III.
evidence: This is based on RMSD analysis.

claim: The presence of a C13 side chain in 2a needs more room for accommodation inside the taxane site compared to baccatin III, which lacks a C13 side chain.
source: This finding can be explained by the presence of a C13 side chain in 2a that needs more room for accommodation inside the taxane site compared to baccatin III, which lacks a C13 side chain.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: A conformational change of the H2' helix was observed in the tubulin-baccatin III structure, which was absent in tubulin-2a.
source: Finally, we observed a conformational change of the H2' helix in the tubulin-baccatin III structure, which was absent in tubulin-2a.
evidence: This is based on RMSD analysis.

claim: Binding of baccatin III to curved tubulin causes a subtle relative twist between the N-terminal and the intermediate domains of β-tubulin.
source: For tubulin-baccatin III, a subtle relative twist between the N-terminal and the intermediate domains was observed (Figure 6; Videos 1 and 2), while binding of 2a rather caused both the N-terminal and intermediate domains of β-tubulin to move slightly apart (Figure 6; Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This is based on structural superposition analysis shown in Figure 6 and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Binding of 2a to curved tubulin causes both the N-terminal and intermediate domains of β-tubulin to move slightly apart.
source: For tubulin-baccatin III, a subtle relative twist between the N-terminal and the intermediate domains was observed (Figure 6; Videos 1 and 2), while binding of 2a rather caused both the N-terminal and intermediate domains of β-tubulin to move slightly apart (Figure 6; Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This is based on structural superposition analysis shown in Figure 6 and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: Taxane binding to tubulin causes global, but subtle conformational rearrangements.
source: Thus, taxane binding to tubulin causes global, but subtle conformational rearrangements.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analyses.

claim: Similar significant conformational changes of both the βT5 and the βM loops were observed upon paclitaxel binding to straight tubulin in microtubules as observed for taxanes bound to curved tubulin.
source: The rmsd analysis revealed similar significant conformational changes of both the βT5 and the βM loops as observed for the taxanes bound to curved tubulin, however, no prominent perturbations of the βS9-βS10 loop could be detected.
evidence: This is based on RMSD analysis comparing paclitaxel-bound and apo microtubules.

claim: No prominent perturbations of the βS9-βS10 loop were detected upon paclitaxel binding to straight tubulin in microtubules.
source: The rmsd analysis revealed similar significant conformational changes of both the βT5 and the βM loops as observed for the taxanes bound to curved tubulin, however, no prominent perturbations of the βS9-βS10 loop could be detected.
evidence: This is based on RMSD analysis.

claim: Significant conformational changes of the 'βS2-βS2'' loop and the C-terminal βH11-βH12 helix region were found upon paclitaxel binding to microtubules, which were not detected in the curved tubulin structures.
source: In addition, we found significant conformational changes of the 'βS2-βS2'' loop (the secondary structural elements that interact with the βM loop of the neighboring protofilament) and the C-terminal βH11-βH12 helix region (Figure 4C and D), which were not detected in the curved tubulin structures.
evidence: This is based on RMSD analysis shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Taxane binding in the context of the microtubule has an effect on the lateral contact established by the βM loop.
source: Together, these results suggest that taxane binding in the context of the microtubule have an effect on the lateral contact established by the βM loop, an effect that cannot be detected in curved tubulin as this contact does not exist in the crystal.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: The tubulin dimer rise increased by 0.24 nm (from 8.12±0.02 to 8.36±0.02 nm) in the presence of GMPCPP compared to GTP.
source: We first analyzed microtubules that were assembled in the presence of either guanosine triphosphate (GTP) (producing GDP-microtubules) or the slowly hydrolyzable GTP analogue GMPCPP (producing GMPCPP-microtubules) and found that the tubulin dimer rise increased by 0.24 nm (from 8.12±0.02 to 8.36±0.02 nm, respectively) in the presence of GMPCPP, a distance that is consistent with that found in previous studies.
evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction measurements reported in Table 2.

claim: The microtubule radius increased from 11.42±0.1 nm for GDP-microtubules to 11.63±0.1 nm for GMPCPP-microtubules.
source: Concomitantly, the microtubule radius increased from 11.42±0.1 nm for GDP-microtubules to 11.63±0.1 nm for GMPCPP-microtubules, which translates into an increase of the average protofilament number (av. PF nr.) from 12.9 to 13.3, respectively.
evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction measurements reported in Table 2.

claim: An increase in both tubulin dimer rise and number of protofilaments for GMPCPP-microtubules compared to GDP-microtubules has been reported previously.
source: An increase in both tubulin dimer rise and number of protofilaments for GMPCPP-microtubules compared to GDP-microtubules has been reported previously (Vale et al., 1994; Alushin et al., 2014; Hyman et al., 1992; Yajima et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Both paclitaxel-bound microtubules and docetaxel-bound microtubules displayed a similar lattice expansion of 0.24 nm as seen for GMPCPP-bound microtubules when compared to GDP-bound microtubules.
source: As shown in Figure 7 and Table 2, and when compared to GDP-bound microtubules, both paclitaxel-bound microtubules and docetaxel-bound microtubules displayed a similar lattice expansion of 0.24 nm as seen for GMPCPP-bound microtubules.
evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction measurements shown in Figure 7 and Table 2.

claim: Paclitaxel-bound microtubules show a reduced microtubule radius of 10.97±0.1 nm (av. PF nr., 12.21).
source: Interestingly, while paclitaxel-bound microtubules show a reduced microtubule radius of 10.97±0.1 nm (av. PF nr., 12.21), docetaxel-bound microtubules displayed a radius of 11.53±0.1 nm (av. PF nr., 12.9), which is similar to the value obtained for GDP-microtubules.
evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction measurements reported in Table 2.

claim: Docetaxel-bound microtubules displayed a radius of 11.53±0.1 nm (av. PF nr., 12.9), which is similar to the value obtained for GDP-microtubules.
source: Interestingly, while paclitaxel-bound microtubules show a reduced microtubule radius of 10.97±0.1 nm (av. PF nr., 12.21), docetaxel-bound microtubules displayed a radius of 11.53±0.1 nm (av. PF nr., 12.9), which is similar to the value obtained for GDP-microtubules.
evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction measurements reported in Table 2.

claim: Lattice expansion by paclitaxel occurred either when the drug was added before the polymerization reaction was started with GTP- or GDP-tubulin, or when it was added to preformed microtubules.
source: In the case of paclitaxel, this expansion occurred either when the drug was added before the polymerization reaction was started with GTP- or GDP-tubulin, or when it was added to preformed microtubules, in consonance with the rapid structural transitions of microtubules observed upon taxane addition (Díaz et al., 1998).
evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction measurements and supported by a literature citation.

claim: Microtubules with bound 2a, 2b, or baccatin III showed similar lattice expansion as those bound to paclitaxel or docetaxel.
source: Interestingly, microtubules with bound 2a, 2b, or baccatin III showed similar lattice expansion as those bound to paclitaxel or docetaxel.
evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction measurements shown in Figure 7 and Table 2.

claim: The diffraction patterns of microtubules stabilized with 2a or 2b showed a diffuse 1 nm layer line that reflects variations in the tubulin monomer rise, in contrast to those bound by paclitaxel and docetaxel, which displayed a sharp band.
source: Note that the diffraction patterns of microtubules stabilized with 2a or 2b showed a diffuse 1 nm layer line that reflects variations in the tubulin monomer (and consequently dimer) rise, in clear contrast to those bound by paclitaxel and docetaxel, which displayed a sharp band, that is, a robust monomer rise.
evidence: This is observed in the X-ray fiber diffraction patterns.

claim: Taxanes with or without a C13 side chain have the capacity to expand the microtubule lattice and thus affect longitudinal tubulin contacts along protofilaments.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that taxanes with or without a C13 side chain have the capacity to expand the microtubule lattice and thus affect longitudinal tubulin contacts along protofilaments.
evidence: This is inferred from the X-ray fiber diffraction results.

claim: The nature of the C13 side chain can affect the radius of a microtubule and thus lateral tubulin contacts between protofilaments.
source: They further indicate that the nature of the C13 side chain can affect the radius of a microtubule and thus lateral tubulin contacts between protofilaments.
evidence: This is inferred from the X-ray fiber diffraction results showing different radii for paclitaxel vs. docetaxel-bound microtubules.

claim: Microtubules assembled in the presence of baccatin III display the same radius as paclitaxel-bound microtubules.
source: We note, however, that microtubules assembled in the presence of baccatin III, which lacks a C13 side chain, display the same radius as paclitaxel-bound microtubules.
evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction measurements reported in Table 2.

claim: The presence of a C13 side chain per se does not seem to modulate lateral tubulin contacts between protofilaments.
source: Thus, the presence of a C13 side chain per se does not seem to modulate lateral tubulin contacts between protofilaments.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that baccatin III (lacking C13 side chain) has the same radius as paclitaxel-bound microtubules.

claim: The βM loop is the most flexible region in MD simulations of the tubulin dimer model.
source: In our simulations of the tubulin dimer model, we found that the βM loop is the most flexible region (Figure 8 top), in good accord with the fact that no density is usually observed for this β-tubulin element in most crystallographic structures.
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Figure 8.

claim: During MD simulations, the βM loop was not structured as an α-helix in any of the models studied; instead, it assumed a relatively stable, extended hairpin conformation that interacted with and blocked access to the taxane site.
source: During the course of the MD simulations, this loop was not structured as an α-helix in any of the models studied; instead, it was found to assume a relatively stable, extended hairpin conformation that interacted with and blocked access to the taxane site.
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results.

claim: When the βM loop was initially modeled as an α-helix, this secondary structure element was rapidly lost during the simulated trajectory regardless of whether or not baccatin III, 2a, or paclitaxel was bound at the taxane site.
source: Even when the βM loop was initially modeled as an α-helix (as present in all microtubule structures solved by cryoelectron microscopy; Alushin et al., 2014; Kellogg et al., 2017; Debs et al., 2020; Manka and Moores, 2018), this secondary structure element was rapidly lost during the simulated trajectory (Figure 8, bottom) regardless of whether or not baccatin III, 2a, or paclitaxel was bound at the taxane site (Figure 9AB).
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: The bound taxanes do not establish any long-lasting hydrogen-bonding interactions with the amino acids making up the βM loop so as to stabilize it into an α-helix, as epothilone A and zampanolide do.
source: One likely reason for this behavior is that the bound taxanes do not establish any long-lasting hydrogen-bonding interactions with the amino acids making up this loop (βL275-βL286) so as to stabilize it into an α-helix, as epothilone A and zampanolide do (Prota et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation results and supported by a literature citation.

claim: The β-hairpin conformation of the βM loop may compete efficiently with the binding of ligands to the taxane site.
source: Therefore, the β-hairpin conformation of the βM loop may compete efficiently with the binding of ligands to the taxane site (Animation 1Animation 1).
evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation results shown in Animation 1.

claim: The free energy of ligand binding to tubulin dimers with a βM loop partially occluding the taxane site would be expected to be much lower (in the 10³–10⁴ M⁻¹ range) than the free energy of binding to microtubules.
source: As a consequence, the free energy of ligand binding to tubulin dimers with a βM loop partially occluding the taxane site would be expected to be much lower (in the 103–104 M–1 range) than the free energy of binding to microtubules, as is indeed the case (Díaz et al., 1993; Canales et al., 2014; Canales et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation results and supported by literature citations.

claim: Paclitaxel can adopt alternatively collapsed conformations in solution that are different from its bioactive, tubulin-bound T-shape conformation.
source: When considering paclitaxel, entry into the taxane site is further hampered by the fact that this bulky and highly hydrophobic molecule can adopt alternatively collapsed conformations in solution that are different from its bioactive, tubulin-bound T-shape conformation (Snyder et al., 2001; Coderch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: The alternative paclitaxel conformations that are inexistent in the case of baccatin III or 2a further reduce the apparent binding affinity below the solubility limit of the ligand.
source: The alternative paclitaxel conformations that are inexistent in the case of baccatin III or 2a further reduce the apparent binding affinity below the solubility limit of the ligand (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation results shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The less stringent requirements of the less bulky baccatin III and 2a molecules to bind compared to paclitaxel may explain the success in obtaining co-crystal structures with tubulin.
source: Conversely, we think that the less stringent requirements of the less bulky baccatin III and 2a molecules to bind as compared to paclitaxel (Figure 10) may explain the success in obtaining co-crystal structures with tubulin.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and MD simulations.

claim: The intermolecular hydrogen bond involving the oxetane O5 and the backbone NH of βT276 is a common feature to all three tubulin-taxane complexes.
source: The intermolecular hydrogen bond involving the oxetane O5 and the backbone NH of βT276 is a common feature to all three tubulin-taxane complexes, both in crystals (baccatin III and 2a) and throughout the simulated MD trajectories (all three ligands).
evidence: This is observed in both crystal structures and MD simulations.

claim: Paclitaxel and 2a establish two other long-lived hydrogen bonds during MD simulations: O4':(NE2)βH229 and O2':(O=C)βR369.
source: Paclitaxel and 2a establish two other long-lived hydrogen bonds during our simulations, namely O4':(NE2)βH229 and O2':(O=C)βR369, which may involve – depending on context – a βR369-βG370 backbone rearrangement.
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results.

claim: The hydroxyl group at C13 of baccatin III alternates between acting as a direct or water-mediated hydrogen bond donor or an acceptor to/from (NE2)βH229 and (O=C)βR369, respectively.
source: In turn, the hydroxyl group at C13 of baccatin III alternates between acting as a direct or water-mediated hydrogen bond donor or an acceptor to/from (NE2)βH229 and (O=C)βR369, respectively.
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results.

claim: Paclitaxel binds better to straight tubulin and promotes tubulin assembly by lowering the critical concentration for tubulin assembly.
source: It has been reported previously that paclitaxel binds better to straight tubulin and promote tubulin assembly (i.e., they lower the critical concentration for tubulin assembly Díaz et al., 1993; Buey et al., 2005) being therefore able to prevent the straight-to-curved conformational transition in GDP-bound microtubules (Elie-Caille et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: MD simulations indicate that protofilaments are curved both in the absence and in the presence of paclitaxel.
source: However, our simulations indicate that protofilaments are curved both in the absence and in the presence of paclitaxel (Figure 9D), which suggests little or no direct influence of taxanes on the straight-to-curved conformational transition of tubulin.
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Figure 9D.

claim: In MD simulations of the taxane-bound protofilament, the occupancy of the taxane site by the ligand constrains the available conformational space of the βM loop compared to that of the apo form, but the loop still fails to adopt a well-defined secondary structure in the absence of additional stabilizing interactions with a neighboring protofilament.
source: On the other hand, and similar to unassembled tubulin, although in our simulations of the taxane-bound protofilament the occupancy of the taxane site by the ligand constrains the available conformational space of the βM loop compared to that of the apo form, the loop still fails to adopt a well-defined secondary structure in the absence of additional stabilizing interactions with a neighboring protofilament.
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results.

claim: The solvent-exposed paclitaxel-bound βM loop is not permanently structured as an α-helix in MD simulations of the minimalist microtubule lattice model.
source: We found that the solvent-exposed paclitaxel-bound βM loop is not permanently structured as an α-helix, as expected, and that the major ligand interactions at site 2 are essentially the same as in the paclitaxel-bound αβ-tubulin heterodimer and the protofilament model (Figure 10).
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Figure 10.

claim: In the interfacial taxane-binding site 1, dispersion forces, additional H-bonds, the hydrophobic effect, and decreased ligand entropy confer to the studied compounds higher binding free energies and longer residence times relative to the tubulin dimer and the exposed taxane site 2.
source: On the other hand, in site 1 dispersion forces, additional H-bonds, the hydrophobic effect, and decreased ligand entropy confer to the studied compounds (paclitaxel, baccatin III, and 2a) higher binding free energies and longer residence times (i.e., lower koff values) relative to the tubulin dimer and the exposed taxane site 2 (Figure 11).
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results and binding energy calculations shown in Figure 11.

claim: The three H-bond-mediated anchoring points O5:(NH)βT276, O4':(NE2)βH229, and O2':(O=C)βR369 are the same as those observed in the microtubule-paclitaxel complex structure.
source: The three H-bond-mediated anchoring points, namely O5:(NH)βT276, O4':(NE2)βH229, and O2':(O=C)βR369, are the same as those observed in the microtubule-paclitaxel complex structure (Kellogg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results and supported by a literature citation.

claim: The hydrogen bond between the amide carbonyl O4' and the imidazole Nε of βHis229 is maintained in all the 2a and paclitaxel complexes studied even though this interaction fluctuates substantially.
source: The hydrogen bond between the amide carbonyl O4' and the imidazole Nε of βHis229 is maintained in all the 2a and paclitaxel complexes studied even though this interaction fluctuates substantially, as does the stacking of βHis229 on the benzoyl phenyl ring.
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results.

claim: The most important interaction that is strengthened laterally when a taxane is bound involves βTyr283, whose position in the βM loop is fixed by segment 85QIFR88 of loop βT3 from the neighboring β-tubulin subunit.
source: However, the most important interaction that is strengthened laterally when a taxane is bound is that involving βTyr283, whose position in the βM loop is fixed by segment 85QIFR88 of loop βT3 from the neighboring β-tubulin subunit, as seen previously for other taxane-site ligands like, for example, zampanolide and taccalonolide AJ (Sánchez-Murcia et al., 2019; Figure 11).
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Figure 11 and supported by a literature citation.

claim: MD simulations consistently reproduce the axial lattice expansion observed upon paclitaxel binding.
source: Importantly, our simulations consistently reproduce the axial lattice expansion observed upon paclitaxel binding (Arnal and Wade, 1995; Alushin et al., 2014; Estévez-Gallego et al., 2020; Kellogg et al., 2017; Debs et al., 2020; Manka and Moores, 2018).
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results and supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: The expansion mainly originates from displacement of the βS9-βS10 loop caused by the Φ/Ψ backbone rearrangement in the βR369-βG370 stretch.
source: We found that the expansion mainly originates from displacement of the βS9-βS10 loop caused by the Φ/Ψ backbone rearrangement in the βR369-βG370 stretch.
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results.

claim: The βS9-βS10 loop acts as a lid covering and stapling the bound taxanes in their final location.
source: Because the βS9-βS10 loop acts as a lid covering and stapling the bound taxanes in their final location, this motion propagates toward the attached α-tubulin subunit so that the distance between the α1- and β2-tubulin subunits of two longitudinally aligned, consecutive tubulin dimers increases by roughly 2 Å as compared to the unbound filament (Figure 9E), a feature that could not be detected in the taxane-bound crystal structures of curved tubulin.
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Figure 9E.

claim: The distance between the α1- and β2-tubulin subunits of two longitudinally aligned, consecutive tubulin dimers increases by roughly 2 Å upon taxane binding as compared to the unbound filament.
source: Because the βS9-βS10 loop acts as a lid covering and stapling the bound taxanes in their final location, this motion propagates toward the attached α-tubulin subunit so that the distance between the α1- and β2-tubulin subunits of two longitudinally aligned, consecutive tubulin dimers increases by roughly 2 Å as compared to the unbound filament (Figure 9E), a feature that could not be detected in the taxane-bound crystal structures of curved tubulin.
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Figure 9E.

claim: The baccatin III core of paclitaxel is responsible for filling most of the taxane site and for the key O5:NH(βT276) hydrogen-bonding interaction that is established between taxanes and β-tubulin.
source: Our results reveal that the baccatin III core of paclitaxel is responsible for filling most of the taxane site and for the key O5:NH(βT276) hydrogen-bonding interaction that is established between taxanes and β-tubulin.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and biochemical results.

claim: The O5:NH(βT276) hydrogen-bonding interaction has only a marginal effect on the drug's microtubule-stabilizing effect.
source: However, this interaction has only a marginal effect on the drug's microtubule-stabilizing effect (Parness et al., 1982; Lataste et al., 1984; Kingston, 2000), which requires the C13 side chain to increase the selectivity of the drugs for microtubules over unassembled tubulin.
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: The C13 side chain is required to increase the selectivity of taxanes for microtubules over unassembled tubulin.
source: However, this interaction has only a marginal effect on the drug's microtubule-stabilizing effect (Parness et al., 1982; Lataste et al., 1984; Kingston, 2000), which requires the C13 side chain to increase the selectivity of the drugs for microtubules over unassembled tubulin.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and biochemical results.

claim: Ring A of paclitaxel precludes binding of the drug to the T2R-TTL and TD1 crystals.
source: On the other hand, we found that ring A of paclitaxel precludes binding of the drug to the T2R-TTL and TD1 crystals, while two taxanes with a modified, smaller C13 side chain (2a and 2b) can bind due to the reduced size of their 3'-acylamino substituents and increased flexibility relative to paclitaxel.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: The smaller substituents of 2a and 2b allow the newly synthesized taxane derivatives to bind to curved, unassembled tubulin while keeping their binding poses very similar to that described for paclitaxel when bound to straight tubulin in microtubules.
source: These smaller substituents allow the newly synthesized taxane derivatives to bind to curved, unassembled tubulin − while keeping their binding poses very similar to that described for paclitaxel when bound to straight tubulin in microtubules − by allowing adaptation of the whole ligand to a rearranged βR369-βG370 backbone in the crystal lattice.
evidence: This is based on the structural results.

claim: The selective recognition of microtubules by taxanes arises from the differential interaction of the bulky C13 side chains with straight and curved tubulin.
source: Regarding the selective recognition of microtubules by taxanes, we found that it arises from two different terms. The first one is the differential interaction of the bulky C13 side chains with straight and curved tubulin.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analyses.

claim: Upon transition to the microtubule-assembled, straight tubulin state, the space around the C13 side chain is narrowed down by the side chains of βD26, βK19, βE22, and βH229 to form a favorable environment for the interaction with ring A, which may lock the paclitaxel-bound tubulin in the straight conformation.
source: Upon transition to the microtubule-assembled, straight tubulin state, this space is narrowed down by the side chains of βD26, βK19, βE22, and βH229 to form a favorable environment for the interaction with ring A, which may lock the paclitaxel-bound tubulin in the straight conformation (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison shown in Figure 12B.

claim: In the absence of the C13 side chain or in the presence of less bulky moieties at the ring A position, ligand binding is likely to be less affected by the curved-to-straight conformational transition.
source: In the absence of the C13 side chain (baccatin III) or in the presence of less bulky and more 'articulated' moieties at the ring A position (2a and 2b; their substituents at the N3 position have a rotatable bond in the middle), ligand binding is likely to be less affected by the curved-to-straight conformational transition, since much looser interactions can still be established with the charged residue side chains of the βS9-βS10 loop and helix H1 through water molecules (Figure 3B, Figure 12A).
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison shown in Figures 3B and 12A.

claim: Occupancy of the taxane site by the βM loop in the absence of lateral contacts is a general mechanism that accounts for the loss of at least four orders of magnitude in affinity when binding to unassembled tubulin relative to microtubules for all taxane-site ligands.
source: A second term that accounts for selectivity is occupancy of the taxane site by the βM loop in the absence of lateral contacts, which would be a general mechanism that accounts for the loss of at least four orders of magnitude in affinity when binding to unassembled tubulin relative to microtubules for all taxane-site ligands, including paclitaxel, docetaxel (Díaz et al., 1993), discodermolide (Canales et al., 2011), epothilones (Canales et al., 2014), and 2a (this paper).
evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation results and supported by literature citations.

claim: In assembled microtubules the βM loop is structured as an α-helix and the preorganized taxane site is empty and ready to accommodate a ligand.
source: Whereas in assembled microtubules the βM loop is structured as an α-helix and the preorganized taxane site is empty and ready to accommodate a ligand, in the unassembled tubulin dimer − as well as in the models of isolated protofilaments and the solvent-exposed site of the minimalist microtubule representation − this same loop displays a large conformational heterogeneity and can adopt a hairpin conformation that allows it to interact with the taxane site and thus to inhibit ligand binding (Figure 11).
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Figure 11.

claim: The conformational freedom of the βM loop in unassembled tubulin allows it to occupy the taxane-binding pocket in such a way as to preclude (or compete with) ligand binding.
source: The MD analysis indicates that the conformational freedom of the βM loop in unassembled tubulin allows it to occupy the taxane-binding pocket in such a way as to preclude (or compete with) ligand binding.
evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation results.

claim: The free energy contribution of taxane-site ligands for microtubule assembly arises from the preferential recognition of the taxane-site conformation present in microtubules.
source: On the other hand, the free energy contribution of taxane-site ligands for microtubule assembly arises from the preferential recognition of the taxane-site conformation present in microtubules (Nogales et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The βM loop is an essential structural element for the mode of action of paclitaxel and other clinically used taxanes.
source: Our results point to the βM loop as an essential structural element for the mode of action of paclitaxel and other clinically used taxanes.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined structural and computational results.

claim: Baccatin III is able to reduce the flexibility of the βM loop by inducing a partial structuring of its N-terminal region.
source: Our high-resolution structural analysis of baccatin III in complex with tubulin suggests that even this simplified taxane is able to reduce the flexibility of the βM loop by inducing a partial structuring of its N-terminal region.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure analysis.

claim: Paclitaxel and the novel taxanes reported here affect interprotofilament contacts so as to promote microtubule stability through interactions with the N-terminal section of the βM loop.
source: This observation suggests that paclitaxel and the novel taxanes reported here indeed affect interprotofilament contacts so as to promote microtubule stability through interactions with the N-terminal section of the βM loop, in good agreement with observations reported previously (Debs et al., 2020; Manka and Moores, 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from X-ray fiber diffraction results and supported by literature citations.

claim: Binding of taxanes to assembled microtubules results in a displacement of the βS9-βS10 loop, which promotes a lattice expansion.
source: Finally, we found that binding of taxanes to assembled microtubules results in a displacement of the βS9-βS10 loop, which promotes a lattice expansion.
evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction data and MD simulations.

claim: Lattice expansion is a general consequence of taxane binding and does not require the presence of a C13 side chain.
source: Our present results reinforce the view that lattice expansion is indeed a general consequence of taxane binding and does not require the presence of a C13 side chain.
evidence: This is based on X-ray fiber diffraction data showing expansion with baccatin III.

claim: Lattice expansion is not an important factor contributing to the mechanism of microtubule stabilization by paclitaxel.
source: Since baccatin III is essentially biologically inert (Parness et al., 1982; Lataste et al., 1984; Kingston, 2000; Andreu and Barasoain, 2001), our data further indicate that lattice expansion is not an important factor contributing to the mechanism of microtubule stabilization by paclitaxel.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that baccatin III causes lattice expansion but is biologically inactive.

claim: In solution, it is the (O=C)βR369 that consistently acts as the hydrogen bond acceptor for the O2' hydroxyl of taxanes.
source: Although in the complexes with 2a and 2b − but not in that with baccatin III − the crystal structures show that (NH)βG370 hydrogen bonds to the taxane side chain, the simulated complexes indicate that in solution it is the (O=C)βR369 that consistently acts as the hydrogen bond acceptor for the O2' hydroxyl of taxanes.
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results.

claim: The βS9-βS10 loop is a major structural element that changes on taxane binding, and this change is transmitted to the following α-tubulin subunits on both sides, hence the stretching or longitudinal expansion of the concatenated tubulin dimers.
source: In our view, these findings point to the βS9-βS10 loop as a major structural element that changes on taxane binding, and this change is transmitted to the following α-tubulin subunits on both sides, hence the stretching or longitudinal expansion of the concatenated tubulin dimers.
evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation results.

claim: The Φ/Ψ backbone rearrangement in the βR369-βG370 stretch upon cooling down the tubulin-paclitaxel and baccatin III complex points to expansion of the cavity and consolidation of the hydrogen-bonding network as the main factors responsible for this conformational change.
source: The fact that we observed the Φ/Ψ backbone rearrangement in the βR369-βG370 stretch upon cooling down the tubulin-paclitaxel and baccatin III complex obtained after the TMD procedure (Animation 2 and Animation 3) points to expansion of the cavity and consolidation of the hydrogen-bonding network as the main factors responsible for this conformational change.
evidence: This is based on MD simulation results shown in Animations 2 and 3.

claim: The core moiety of paclitaxel provides the main tubulin-interaction network while its C13 side chain enables selective recognition of the prestructured βM loop of the microtubule-assembled tubulin state.
source: Our structural analyses further suggest a mode of action of paclitaxel by means of which its core moiety provides the main tubulin-interaction network while its C13 side chain enables selective recognition of the prestructured βM loop of the microtubule-assembled tubulin state.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined structural and computational results.

claim: Differential recognition of the prestructured βM loop by the C13 side chain is expected to promote microtubule formation and stabilization.
source: Such differential recognition is expected to promote microtubule formation and stabilization.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and computational results.

claim: The longitudinal expansion of the microtubule lattices is not related to the microtubule stabilization mechanism of taxanes.
source: On the other hand, the longitudinal expansion of the microtubule lattices arises from the accommodation of the taxane core within the site, a process that is, however, not related to the microtubule stabilization mechanism of taxanes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that baccatin III causes expansion but is inactive.
